categories.name: Creational Patterns
categories.description: Abstract the object creation process, decoupling a system from how its objects are created, composed, and represented.

patterns.name: Abstract Factory
patterns.intent: Provide an interface for creating families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes.
patterns.problem: You need to create families of related products (e.g. buttons and menus of one theme) while guaranteeing that products of one family are never mixed with products of another.
patterns.solution: Declare an abstract factory with one method per product. Concrete factories implement it, creating products of a specific theme/variant. The client works only with interfaces.
applicability: A system class must automatically pick a product configuration
You need to ensure compatibility of products within one family
The system should work with unknown product families via a common interface
cons: Hard to add new product kinds to existing factories
More interfaces and abstraction layers

code.title: GUI themes

patterns.name: Builder
patterns.intent: Separates the construction of a complex object from its representation so the same process can create different representations.
patterns.problem: Object construction balloons with optional parameters and invariant checks, leading to telescoping constructors.
patterns.solution: Extract assembly into a separate builder with a chain of With... methods and a final Build() that validates invariants.
applicability: Constructing complex objects with options and constraints
The same assembly process must produce different representations
An immutable result is required
cons: More code for simple objects
The builder often knows product internals

code.title: Combo meal

patterns.name: Prototype
patterns.intent: Creates new objects by copying an existing prototype instance.
patterns.problem: Building an object from scratch is expensive or requires private state; similar configurations must be produced quickly.
patterns.solution: Implement a Clone() method that copies object state (deeply for lists/dictionaries) and produce new instances from the prototype.
applicability: Avoid subclassing just for parameterization
Copy complex object graphs
Create objects without knowing their concrete classes
pros: Works with unknown classes through an abstraction
cons: Deep copy is non-trivial (cycles)
Hidden references are easy to forget when cloning

code.title: Report templates

patterns.name: Singleton
patterns.intent: Guarantees a single instance of a class and provides a global access point to it.
patterns.problem: Exactly one instance of a resource (config, logger, pool) must exist and be reachable from anywhere.
patterns.solution: Seal the constructor and expose a static Instance property initialized once in a thread-safe way.
applicability: Exactly one controlled instance
A single control point over a shared resource
cons: Global state complicates testing
Hidden dependencies between modules
Violates SRP if it holds behavior

code.title: Application configuration

patterns.name: Factory Method
patterns.intent: Defines an interface for creating objects but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate.
patterns.problem: A class cannot know upfront which product subtypes to create yet wants to centralize common workflow code around them.
patterns.solution: Extract product creation into a protected abstract factory method; subclasses override it to return the desired product.
applicability: A class does not know product types upfront
A library wants to offer extension points to users
Reuse logic across different products
pros: New products are easy to add
cons: Each product needs its own subclass
Deeper hierarchy than plain new

code.title: Log sources

patterns.name: Dependency Injection
patterns.intent: Supplies an object's dependencies from the outside (via constructor) instead of letting it create them itself.
patterns.problem: A class creates its concrete dependencies itself, making reuse and testing with substitutes (e.g. clocks) impossible.
patterns.solution: Describe dependencies as interfaces, accept them via the constructor, and compose the object in a DI container.
applicability: Testability via substitute dependencies
Swap implementations without touching clients
Explicit class contracts
cons: Container infrastructure for trivial cases
Risk of drifting toward a service locator

code.title: Report service with clocks

categories.name: Structural Patterns
categories.description: Compose objects and classes into larger structures while keeping them flexible and efficient.

patterns.name: Adapter
patterns.intent: Make an object with one interface usable through another, expected interface.
patterns.problem: A useful class exists, but its interface does not match the client's interface. Neither the client nor the class can be rewritten.
patterns.solution: Create an adapter class that implements the client's target interface and translates calls to the adaptee's methods (via composition).
applicability: You want to reuse an existing class whose interface doesn't fit
Several unrelated classes should serve one common interface
Working with legacy/third-party libraries without changing their code
pros: Client is decoupled from a concrete API
Multiple services can be wrapped behind one interface
cons: An extra level of indirection
Code gets harder to read over time

code.title: Wrapping a legacy SDK

patterns.name: Bridge
patterns.intent: Decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently.
patterns.problem: A tight coupling between an abstraction and its implementations explodes the number of subclasses whenever a new platform or variant is added.
patterns.solution: The abstraction keeps a reference to an implementation object (interface) and delegates work to it. Both sides evolve independently behind a common contract.
applicability: Detach abstraction from implementation (cross-platform)
Swap implementations at runtime
Two orthogonal axes of variation (shape × drawing API)
pros: Behavior substitution without rebuilding the hierarchy
cons: Extra complexity due to two hierarchies
Clients must be aware of both hierarchies

code.title: Shapes over different graphics APIs

patterns.name: Composite
patterns.intent: Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies, letting clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly.
patterns.problem: Clients need to process both single objects and groups of objects, duplicating logic for each kind while tree traversal gets messy.
patterns.solution: A common component interface is implemented by leaves and containers alike. A container holds child components and recursively delegates operations to them.
applicability: Domain naturally forms a tree (folders, UI, menus)
Uniform treatment of single objects and compositions
Single place for recursive traversal
pros: One interface for leaves and containers
New component types are easy to add
cons: Hard to restrict the composition's component types
Over-generalized interface for specialized operations

code.title: Boxes and items inside

patterns.name: Decorator
patterns.intent: Dynamically adds new behavior to an object by wrapping it in a decorator object with the same interface.
patterns.problem: Subclassing for every behavioral variant produces a huge class count that cannot be combined freely.
patterns.solution: A decorator class holds a reference to the wrapped object, implements the same interface and augments/overrides its behavior. Decorators stack in any order.
applicability: Add/remove behavior on the fly
Direct inheritance is impractical (sealed classes)
Free combination of toppings
pros: More flexible than inheritance via composition
New behavior without touching existing classes
cons: Many tiny wrapper objects
Debugging decorator chains takes care

code.title: Sprucing up notifications

patterns.name: Facade
patterns.intent: Provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem of many classes, hiding its inner workings.
patterns.problem: Clients must interact directly with many interdependent subsystem classes, knowing their sequence and contracts.
patterns.solution: A single facade class encapsulates typical scenarios against the subsystem and exposes a few simple methods.
applicability: Simple entry point into a complex library/subsystem
Layer separation (UI ← facade → domain services)
Building an API over scattered modules
cons: Facade may grow into a god object
No direct access to advanced subsystem features

code.title: Single entry point to the conversion pipeline

patterns.name: Proxy
patterns.intent: Supplies a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it, adding laziness, caching or protection.
patterns.problem: Direct access to an object is undesirable: it is too expensive, remote, or requires permission checks.
patterns.solution: The proxy implements the same interface as the real subject, intercepts calls and decides whether to forward them, serve from cache, or deny.
applicability: Lazy initialization of heavy resources
Caching frequent requests
Access control / authorization, remote proxies (RPC)
pros: Clients keep using the same interface
Access control and optimization without changing the real object
cons: Extra indirection layer
Cache/invalidation complexity

code.title: Caching proxy to an external API

categories.name: Behavioral Patterns
categories.description: Distribute responsibility and communication algorithms between objects.

patterns.name: Strategy
patterns.intent: Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable.
patterns.problem: There are several behavior variants that must be selected or switched at runtime. Hard-coding all variants with if/else in one class is a bad idea.
patterns.solution: Extract each behavior into its own class sharing a common interface. The context keeps a strategy reference and delegates work to it.
applicability: Many similar classes differ only by behavior
Algorithm details should be hidden from the client
The algorithm is chosen dynamically (settings, A/B tests, platform)
pros: Open/Closed: a new variant is a new class
cons: The client must know about strategy differences
Growth in the number of small classes
